articles.title: This Year Has Fifty Three Weeks and Last Time Our Reports Lost One of Them
articles.excerpt: Most of our reporting is by week. Depots are measured on weekly sales, buyers forecast in weeks, and the board pack compares each week with the same week last year. Under the standard week numbering t…
articles.body: Most of our reporting is by week. Depots are measured on weekly sales, buyers forecast in weeks, and the board pack compares each week with the same week last year. Under the standard week numbering that most of our systems use, a year has fifty two weeks, except now and then, when it has fifty three. This year is one of those. Week fifty three of 2026 starts on Monday the twenty eighth of December. The last such year was 2020, and we found out the hard way. Our sales data warehouse had a table of weeks built in 2015, with fifty two rows for every year, and the overnight load looked up the week for each sale in that table. For the last week of 2020 it found nothing, and it quietly discarded the rows.
articles.author: Serguey Shinder

articles.excerpt: This post covers saving test flows as agent-device .ad scripts and running them again, using a Flutter app. It goes through writing an .ad file, getting the app into the right state before a replay, r…
articles.body: This post covers saving test flows as agent-device .ad scripts and running them again, using a Flutter app. It goes through writing an .ad file, getting the app into the right state before a replay, reading the report when a replay stops and fixing it, and the token cost of agent-driven QA. It is based on agent-device 0.21.31 (2026-10-25). Installation and the basic loop are in Part 1 , and real-device setup is in Part 2 . What an .ad file is When an agent checks an app, it reads the screen, picks the next thing to tap, and reads the result, over and over. Exploring the same flow this way every time keeps costing time and tokens. An .ad file pins down the result of that exploration as a list of commands, and replay runs the list from top to bottom.

articles.title: This Box's Homepage Named Its Own CVE — Ignite (TryHackMe)
articles.excerpt: Platform: TryHackMe · Difficulty: Easy · Category: Fuel CMS RCE / Credential Reuse The page title says "Welcome to FUEL CMS." Not a generic landing page, not a logo with no text — the literal CMS name…
articles.body: Platform: TryHackMe · Difficulty: Easy · Category: Fuel CMS RCE / Credential Reuse Introduction The page title says "Welcome to FUEL CMS." Not a generic landing page, not a logo with no text — the literal CMS name, in the <title> tag, for anyone running curl to read. That's either refreshingly honest or a significant operational security failure, and either way it meant I could skip version fingerprinting entirely and go straight to searchsploit . Ignite carries a well-documented unauthenticated RCE in Fuel CMS 1.4.1, and once that door opens, the rest of the box leans on a mistake seen constantly in real engagements: a database credential, sitting in plaintext in a configuration file, reused verbatim as the root system password.

If you build web tools, you know that keeping them accessible is a constant challenge. When we launched the RahaLune QR Code Templates Library, it was a fully functional, client-side React application with over 100 pre-designed templates. Users could browse templates, open a modal editor, customize colors, and download high-resolution QR codes. But there was a glaring problem: it was English-only. For a tool designed to help global businesses, this was a massive barrier to entry. Today, we rolled out a massive update.

articles.title: What a real user's USB capture found that my synthetic tests didn't: two bugs in usb-rea
articles.excerpt: For weeks every test of usb-rea ran on captures I generated myself, on protocols documented by liquidctl and rivalcfg, and on a few public Wireshark samples. All of that passed. Then a real user share…
articles.body: For weeks every test of usb-rea ran on captures I generated myself, on protocols documented by liquidctl and rivalcfg, and on a few public Wireshark samples. All of that passed. Then a real user shared a real capture, and within a day it had found two bugs that none of my tests could have found. This is the fifth post about usb-rea, an open-source tool I built that diffs USB captures per labelled click in a vendor app and writes a pyusb driver. The first one covered commands, the second one naming what the device reports back, the third one handshakes and session tokens, the fourth one video streams to case LCDs. This one is about what happened when the tool met hardware I don't own.

articles.title: Your Code Is About to Run in a Hospital
articles.excerpt: Your team has won a contract, and the feature you have been building for three months will go live on a hospital ward next month. Nurses will use it to see which patients are due their medication. Som…
articles.body: Your team has won a contract, and the feature you have been building for three months will go live on a hospital ward next month. Nurses will use it to see which patients are due their medication. Somewhere in the last week this stopped feeling like a project and started feeling like a weight. What if you got something wrong? That feeling is not a sign you are the wrong person for the job. It is a sign you understand what the job is. The engineers I would worry about are the ones who feel nothing at all. The task is not to make the fear go away. It is to turn it into something useful. Start by writing your worries down. Not a vague dread, but specific questions. What happens if the network drops halfway through an update? What does a nurse see if two people change the same record?

articles.title: This Android gaming benchmark app does something I’ve never seen before
articles.excerpt: Evolve is a new gaming benchmark that shows you where mobile GPUs are hitting a bottleneck.
articles.body: Credit: Harish Jonnalagadda / Android Authority I like benchmarks a little too much and use them on every new phone I test. Synthetic benchmarks like Geekbench and 3DMark do a good job of simulating real-world usage and gaming scenarios, and they predict a device’s performance potential reasonably well. As someone who gets over 75 phones a year, a synthetic benchmark lets me easily measure how a particular device holds up against its predecessor. There’s a new benchmark that aims to go beyond just delivering an overall score. It’s called Evolve , and it provides useful insights across five metrics, allowing you to then pinpoint which part of the GPU is handling modern workloads well, and what’s causing a potential bottleneck.

articles.excerpt: From a close encounter between Mars and Jupiter to dazzling Venus and elusive Mercury, November offers plenty of planetary highlights. Here's when and where to look.
articles.body: This is a great month for planet watching, either in the evenings or mornings. During convenient evening hours, the planet of choice is Saturn , visible well up in the southern sky during mid-to-late evening hours. Telescopically, the southern side of its famous ring system is currently tilted about 6½ degrees to our line of sight. Around the middle of the night, Mars and Jupiter come into view above the east-northeast horizon and just before the break of dawn are in excellent position, soaring high in the southern sky in the vicinity of the Sickle of Leo the Lion. Watch how Mars approaches Jupiter early in the month, passes it on Nov. 16, then spends the rest of the month sailing away to the east.

articles.title: 9 nightmarish sci-fi spaceships to crawl aboard for Halloween if you dare
articles.excerpt: Grab your high-lumen flashlight and gargantuan gun to explore these vicious vessels
articles.body: Abandoned, possessed, or infested spaceships in sci-fi films, books, and video games are usually not a welcoming place to hang your helmet and kick back inside. Many are distinctly marked as DO NOT APPROACH zones and equipped with clearly articulated warning messages to keep your distance, but that doesn't ever seem to stop scavengers, space pirates, or evil industrial mega corporations from waving off these dangerous signs to board anyway. Other creaky craft are apt to contain nasty alien hitchhikers or biological hazards not exactly conducive to a pleasant star-trekking voyage. Whether these nefarious neglected craft have just reappeared from the other side of a black hole or have been lying dormant for eons on a hostile planetoid, visitors are usually infrequent.

articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
